value.overview: The Great Jacamar (Jacamerops aureus) is the largest and most robust member of the jacamar family. It is a forest-dwelling insectivore with glossy green and blue-iridescent upperparts, rich rufous underparts, a long thick black bill, and a relatively long tail. Usually encountered alone or in pairs, it often remains motionless on a shaded perch before making short flights to capture prey. Its broad distribution extends from Costa Rica south through much of northern and western South America.
value.classification: The Great Jacamar belongs to the family Galbulidae in the order Piciformes. It is the only species in the genus Jacamerops.
value.identification: This large jacamar measures about 25–30 cm long and has a notably heavy body and thick, slightly downcurved black bill. Adults show glossy metallic green on the head, face, and upperparts, with blue or coppery reflections on the crown, throat, back, and tail. The underparts are mainly deep rufous, while the flight feathers are dark. Males have a conspicuous white lower throat; females generally lack or have less of this white area. Immatures are duller and less richly colored.
value.rangeHabitat: The Great Jacamar occurs from Costa Rica and Panama through Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Venezuela, the Guianas, and Brazil. In Costa Rica it is a rare to very uncommon resident of the Caribbean lowlands and foothills, generally from sea level to about 500 m. It is reported particularly from the northern Caribbean region, including the San Carlos and Tortuguero plains. It uses humid lowland forest, tall shaded second growth, forest edges, clearings, and areas along streams, usually in the middle and lower canopy.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and across its range; it is not considered a regular long-distance migrant. Local movements may occur, especially after breeding or when birds disperse.
value.breeding: Breeding has been recorded in Costa Rica mainly from March through May or June. The pair excavates a chamber in an arboreal termite mound, usually about 3–15 m above the ground; cavities in suitable decaying wood have also been reported. Both parents participate in incubation and care of the young. Available information on clutch size, incubation, and nestling development is limited, so detailed breeding behavior remains poorly documented.
value.dietFeeding: The Great Jacamar eats mainly insects, including beetles, butterflies and moths, wasps, bees, ants, dragonflies, and other flying or arboreal insects. It commonly waits on a shaded branch and makes short sallies to seize prey in the air, but unlike many jacamars it also gleans prey from vegetation. Spiders and occasional small lizards have been recorded, including in Costa Rica. Prey may be beaten against a branch before being swallowed.
value.behavior: This species is usually seen singly or in pairs and may sit quietly for long periods, making it difficult to detect in dense forest. It favors shaded perches in the canopy and at forest openings, from which it watches for passing insects. Pairs may maintain territories around suitable feeding and nesting sites. Its flight is generally brief and direct between perches, and its iridescent plumage is most evident in good light or during close views.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, but the species has an extremely large range and the decline is not currently believed to approach the threshold for a threatened category.
